title: 221. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Inequalities Involving Logarithmic Functions
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with base greater than \(1\)
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_2(x-1)>3\) by converting to exponential form and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x-1)>3\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\). Since the base \(2\) is greater than \(1\), the logarithmic function is increasing. Therefore \(\log_2(x-1)>3\) implies \(x-1>2^3=8\), so \(x>9\). Combining \(x>1\) with \(x>9\) gives \(x>9\).
questions.hint: Convert the logarithmic inequality to exponential form, and remember that the argument of the logarithm must be positive.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with base between \(0\) and \(1\)
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_{\frac{1}{2}}(x+3)\ge -1\) by reversing the inequality and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_{\frac{1}{2}}(x+3)\ge -1\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(x+3>0\), so \(x>-3\). Since the base \(\frac{1}{2}\) is between \(0\) and \(1\), the logarithmic function is decreasing. Therefore \(\log_{\frac{1}{2}}(x+3)\ge -1\) implies \(x+3\le \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}=2\), so \(x\le -1\). Combining \(x>-3\) with \(x\le -1\) gives \(-3<x\le -1\).
questions.hint: When the base is between \(0\) and \(1\), the inequality direction reverses when converting to exponential form.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with base greater than \(1\)
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_3(x+2)<2\) by converting to exponential form and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x+2)<2\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(x+2>0\), so \(x>-2\). Since the base \(3\) is greater than \(1\), the logarithmic function is increasing. Therefore \(\log_3(x+2)<2\) implies \(x+2<3^2=9\), so \(x<7\). Combining \(x>-2\) with \(x<7\) gives \(-2<x<7\).
questions.hint: Convert the inequality to exponential form, then intersect the result with the domain condition.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with base between \(0\) and \(1\)
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}}(2x-1)>1\) by reversing the inequality and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}}(2x-1)>1\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(2x-1>0\), so \(x>\frac{1}{2}\). Since the base \(\frac{1}{3}\) is between \(0\) and \(1\), the logarithmic function is decreasing. Therefore \(\log_{\frac{1}{3}}(2x-1)>1\) implies \(2x-1<\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^1=\frac{1}{3}\), so \(2x<\frac{4}{3}\), and \(x<\frac{2}{3}\). Combining \(x>\frac{1}{2}\) with \(x<\frac{2}{3}\) gives \(\frac{1}{2}<x<\frac{2}{3}\).
questions.hint: Reverse the inequality direction when the base is between \(0\) and \(1\), then apply the domain condition.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities using logarithm laws
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x+2)>2\) by using the product law and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x+2)>2\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x-1>0\) and \(x+2>0\), so \(x>1\). Using the product law,
\[
\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x+2)=\log_2[(x-1)(x+2)]
\]
The inequality becomes \(\log_2[(x-1)(x+2)]>2\). Since the base \(2\) is greater than \(1\), we get \((x-1)(x+2)>2^2=4\). Expanding gives \(x^2+x-2>4\), so \(x^2+x-6>0\). Factoring gives \((x+3)(x-2)>0\), so \(x<-3\) or \(x>2\). Combining with \(x>1\) gives \(x>2\).
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms using the product law, solve the resulting quadratic inequality, and intersect with the domain condition.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with a quadratic argument
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_{0.5}(x^2-4)\le -2\) by reversing the inequality and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_{0.5}(x^2-4)\le -2\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(x^2-4>0\), so \(x<-2\) or \(x>2\). Since the base \(0.5\) is between \(0\) and \(1\), the logarithmic function is decreasing. Therefore \(\log_{0.5}(x^2-4)\le -2\) implies \(x^2-4\ge (0.5)^{-2}=4\), so \(x^2\ge 8\). Thus \(x\le -2\sqrt{2}\) or \(x\ge 2\sqrt{2}\). These values automatically satisfy \(x<-2\) or \(x>2\), so the solution is \(x\le -2\sqrt{2}\) or \(x\ge 2\sqrt{2}\).
questions.hint: Reverse the inequality direction because the base is between \(0\) and \(1\), then solve the resulting quadratic inequality and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with logarithms on both sides
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_3(x-1)\le \log_3(5-x)\) by comparing arguments and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x-1)\le \log_3(5-x)\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(x-1>0\) and \(5-x>0\), so \(1<x<5\). Since the base \(3\) is greater than \(1\), the logarithmic function is increasing. Therefore \(\log_3(x-1)\le \log_3(5-x)\) implies \(x-1\le 5-x\). Solving gives \(2x\le 6\), so \(x\le 3\). Combining with \(1<x<5\) gives \(1<x\le 3\).
questions.hint: Compare the arguments because the bases are the same and greater than \(1\), then intersect the result with the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with base between \(0\) and \(1\)
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_{\frac{1}{2}}(x+1)\ge \log_{\frac{1}{2}}(2x-3)\) by reversing the inequality and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_{\frac{1}{2}}(x+1)\ge \log_{\frac{1}{2}}(2x-3)\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(x+1>0\) and \(2x-3>0\), so \(x>\frac{3}{2}\). Since the base \(\frac{1}{2}\) is between \(0\) and \(1\), the logarithmic function is decreasing. Therefore \(\log_{\frac{1}{2}}(x+1)\ge \log_{\frac{1}{2}}(2x-3)\) implies \(x+1\le 2x-3\). Solving gives \(4\le x\), so \(x\ge 4\). Combining with \(x>\frac{3}{2}\) gives \(x\ge 4\).
questions.hint: Reverse the inequality because the base is between \(0\) and \(1\), then solve the resulting linear inequality and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities using logarithm laws
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_2(x+3)+\log_2(x-1)\le 3\) by using the product law and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x+3)+\log_2(x-1)\le 3\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+3>0\) and \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\). Using the product law,
\[
\log_2(x+3)+\log_2(x-1)=\log_2[(x+3)(x-1)]
\]
The inequality becomes \(\log_2[(x+3)(x-1)]\le 3\). Since the base \(2\) is greater than \(1\), we get \((x+3)(x-1)\le 2^3=8\). Expanding gives \(x^2+2x-3\le 8\), so \(x^2+2x-11\le 0\). The roots are \(x=-1\pm 2\sqrt{3}\), so \(-1-2\sqrt{3}\le x\le -1+2\sqrt{3}\). Combining with \(x>1\) gives \(1<x\le -1+2\sqrt{3}\).
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms using the product law, solve the resulting quadratic inequality, and intersect with the domain condition.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic inequalities with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\log_3(x+2)>\log_9(x+8)\) by converting to a common base and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x+2)>\log_9(x+8)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+2>0\) and \(x+8>0\), so \(x>-2\). Convert \(\log_9(x+8)\) to base \(3\), and the inequality becomes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_9(x+8) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(x+8)\\
\log_3(x+2) &> \frac{1}{2}\log_3(x+8)
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying by \(2\) gives \(2\log_3(x+2)>\log_3(x+8)\), so \(\log_3[(x+2)^2]>\log_3(x+8)\). Since the base \(3\) is greater than \(1\), we get \((x+2)^2>x+8\). Expanding gives \(x^2+4x+4>x+8\), so \(x^2+3x-4>0\). Factoring gives \((x+4)(x-1)>0\), so \(x<-4\) or \(x>1\). Combining with \(x>-2\) gives \(x>1\).
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(9\) logarithm to base \(3\), then compare the arguments and intersect with the domain condition.
